comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 66: byte-level aux loss, and what DeepSeek V4.1's attention offers us** (for your comments on [byte targets](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5858745269) and DeepSeek V4.1; d512, equal steps, on candidate 2 = 3.0197)

Also: sorry about the stray links. My comments had bare `#NNN` references to Parameter Golf and modded-nanogpt PRs, which GitHub resolved to marin issues. I've fixed 14 comments and the Status table, and those references are now full links or code-quoted.

**Byte-level aux loss** (`byte_aux_bytes`, `08a27af3ab`; the tokenizer is read, never changed):
- `train.py` builds a `[vocab, 8]` table of each token's first 8 UTF-8 bytes (−1 past its end), using the same `decode([".", id])` prefix trick as the BPB eval, with `<0xNN>` byte tokens handled. It logs mean length and truncation stats. On the gpt2 tokenizer, 21.7% of tokens are longer than 8 bytes.
- A separate head `[D, 8·256]` on the final hidden state (the lm_head input) predicts the *next* token's bytes, 256-way per position.
- The weight decays linearly from `byte_aux_weight` to 0 at 50% of training, as you said. Once it reaches 0, a `lax.cond` skips the head entirely, so it only costs anything in the first half.
- On CPU the byte loss starts at ln 256 and gets gradients, and weight 0 skips it.
- Runs: weight 0.1 and 0.3.

**DeepSeek V4 / V4.1 attention** (a research pass read the [V4 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348), the [V4.1 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19969), V3.2's DSA and the HF inference code):
- **What they are:**
  - V3.2's DSA is a lightning indexer (64 ReLU-scored heads) that picks top-2048 tokens.
  - V4 adds CSA (softmax-gated compression at m = 4 plus a top-k indexer) and HCA (m = 128, dense), alternating across layers. Every layer also has a 128-token sliding window and a learnable per-head sink, and the query uses shared K = V MQA over 512-dim heads.
  - V4.1 simplifies this to CSA2, with KV and index reuse across layers and a YOCO-like encoder-decoder split. It **drops per-head Q-norm, keeps KV RMSNorm, and makes Muon head-wise for W_q / W_k.**
- **Why most of it doesn't fit us:** it is built for 1M-token contexts, KV memory and inference FLOPs. At seq 4096 with 2 global MLA layers, an indexer costs about what it prunes, and the papers claim quality *parity* at best, after long dense warm-ups. No ablations are published.
- **What does fit:**
  1. **Head-wise Muon for the attention projections:** V4.1's pick, with GLM-5 and Kimi-K3 cited. We tried per-head Muon in [batch 3](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5840199301) (+0.0018 on the old base); it's config-only (`muon_head_dim=128`), so it's retested here on candidate 2.
  2. **A learnable per-head attention sink on the 2 MLA layers:** FA4 supports `learnable_sink` upstream. It needs our FA4 bridge to expose it, next to the relative-bias score-mod. Our per-head output gate already covers most of what a sink does, so the expected gain is small.
  3. **K-only RMSNorm (no Q-norm) on MLA:** V4.1's final setup. Worth one run, given that QK-norm clashed with our MLA setup.
  4. **Pure SWA-128 softmax in layer 0 instead of KDA:** both V4s use SWA first layers, mainly as a throughput choice. This needs a third layer type.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| byte aux loss, 8 bytes, weight 0.1 → 0 at 50% | [`08a27af3ab`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/08a27af3ab) | [lc1-b66-byte01](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b66-byte01) | 2817 | 720 | 3.2434 | 3.0209 | +0.0012 vs 3.0197 |
| byte aux loss, 8 bytes, weight 0.3 → 0 at 50% | [`08a27af3ab`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/08a27af3ab) | [lc1-b66-byte03](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b66-byte03) | 2817 | 719 | 3.2532 | 3.0274 | +0.0077 vs 3.0197 |
| head-wise Muon on attention projections (V4.1; retest) | [`08a27af3ab`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/08a27af3ab) | [lc1-b66-headmuon](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b66-headmuon) | 2817 | 726 | 3.2559 | 3.0251 | +0.0054 vs 3.0197 |
| MLA key-only RMSNorm (V4.1), `mla_k_norm` | [`5918812913`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5918812913) | [lc1-b66-knorm](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b66-knorm) | 2817 | 727 | 3.2386 | 3.0139 | −0.0058 vs 3.0197 |

**Results:**
- **Byte-level aux loss hurts, and more with weight:** +0.0012 at 0.1 and **+0.0077 at 0.3**.
  - The byte head reads the *final* hidden state, the lm_head's input. During the first half of training it pulls that representation toward byte-predictive features, in the steps where the main objective is learning fastest. The damage doesn't fully recover after the weight reaches 0 at step ~1400.
  - The loss was live as designed: the byte head's gradient is nonzero until step ~1400 and exactly 0 after.
  - **Informed variant (next):** attach the byte head to a mid-network hidden state, so the byte signal shapes lower-level features without taxing the lm_head input. I'll also log the byte loss so its trajectory is visible.
- **Head-wise Muon on the attention projections: +0.0054** on candidate 2 (it was +0.0018 on the batch-3 base). Our attention heads are few (4 × 128 at d512) and share the NoPE logit scale and relative bias, so orthogonalizing per head seems to throw away useful cross-head structure in the update. Not adopted.

**Informed variant queued** (`7e05733234`): `byte_aux_mid_layer` feeds the byte head the RMS-normed **mid-network AttnRes stream** (the embedding plus the first half of the completed blocks) instead of the lm_head input. The byte loss is now logged as `train/aux/byte_loss`.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| byte aux from the mid-network stream, weight 0.1 | [`7e05733234`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/7e05733234) | [lc1-b66-bytemid01](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b66-bytemid01) | 2817 | 723 | 3.2503 | 3.0277 | +0.0080 vs 3.0197 |
| byte aux from the mid-network stream, weight 0.3 | [`7e05733234`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/7e05733234) | [lc1-b66-bytemid03](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b66-bytemid03) | 2817 | 716 | 3.2623 | 3.0372 | +0.0175 vs 3.0197 |

**MLA key-only RMSNorm: −0.0058**, the largest single gain since candidate 2.
- The learned MLA logit scale follows almost the same path with and without it (3.48 / 3.44 → 3.59 / 3.61 at the end on layers 3 / 5), so this isn't a temperature change.
- Normalizing the keys removes per-token key-*magnitude* variation. Without it, a key with a large norm wins attention regardless of its direction. With it, the logit is query magnitude × key direction.
- **Mechanism-informed variant:** our partial key offset makes half of each key's channels come from the previous token, so a single norm over the whole key still lets whichever half is larger dominate. `mla_k_norm_split` (`a69864fc13`) normalizes the previous-token half and the current-token half separately.
- **Seed noise:** candidate 2's seeds are 3.0197 / 3.0266 / **3.0274** (seed 2 from batch 67; mean 3.0246), so seed 0 was a lucky draw. Replicates are paired per seed.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MLA key-only RMSNorm, seed 1 | [`a69864fc13`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a69864fc13) | [lc1-b66-knorm-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b66-knorm-s1) | 2817 | 727 | 3.2442 | 3.0203 | −0.0063 vs 3.0266 |
| MLA key-only RMSNorm, seed 2 | [`a69864fc13`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a69864fc13) | [lc1-b66-knorm-s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b66-knorm-s2) | 2817 | 723 | 3.2471 | 3.0228 | −0.0046 vs 3.0274 |
| key norm split over the offset halves | [`a69864fc13`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a69864fc13) | [lc1-b66-knorm-split](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b66-knorm-split) | 2817 | 726 | 3.2374 | 3.0150 | −0.0047 vs 3.0197 |

**Mid-network byte head: worse.** +0.0080 at weight 0.1 and +0.0175 at 0.3, against +0.0012 / +0.0077 from the final hidden. The byte loss is now logged:

| step | 0 | 350 | 700 | 1050 | 1400 (weight → 0) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| byte loss, weight 0.1 (nats/byte) | 5.65 (= ln 256) | 1.93 | 1.82 | 1.86 | off |
| byte loss, weight 0.3 (nats/byte) | 5.65 | 1.72 | 1.61 | 1.63 | off |

- The model does learn the target's bytes: it is down to about 1.7 nats per byte within 350 steps.
- **That learning costs the main loss, and costs it more the deeper the byte signal enters.** Mid-network features feed every later layer, so byte-shaping them interferes more than shaping the lm_head input. At a 16k vocab, the lm_head input already carries the byte structure the next-token loss needs.
- **Last informed tweak:** keep only an *early* dose, weight 0.1 decaying to 0 by 20% of training, on the final hidden. That tests whether early byte supervision helps organize the embedding space before the interference matters. If it's neutral too, the branch closes at d512.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| byte aux, final hidden, weight 0.1 → 0 by 20% | [`03ee1a03d5`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/03ee1a03d5) | [lc1-b66-byte-early](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b66-byte-early) | 2817 | 719 | 3.2437 | 3.0222 | +0.0025 vs 3.0197 |

**MLA key-only RMSNorm replicates on 3 seeds: −0.0058 / −0.0063 / −0.0046 (mean −0.0056, k ≈ 1.036×)** at no ex/s cost. It is adopted: **candidate 3 = candidate 2 + `mla_k_norm`.**
- The split variant (the previous-token and current-token halves normalized separately) is −0.0047, no better than one norm over the whole key. Magnitude imbalance *between* the offset halves wasn't the issue; per-token key magnitude as a whole was.
- **Why it works where QK-norm didn't:** normalizing the *query* too took away the query-magnitude temperature that the learnable qk_mult and the Inkling bias rely on. Keys only lose a nuisance degree of freedom: a large-norm key winning regardless of content.

**Early-only byte loss (weight 0.1 → 0 by 20%, final hidden): +0.0025.** Even a short early dose doesn't help, so early byte supervision doesn't speed up how the embedding space gets organized either. Across all five configurations the byte objective is neutral to harmful, and the harm grows with its weight and with how deep it enters:

| byte loss | weight 0.1 | weight 0.3 |
|---|---|---|
| final hidden, off at 50% | +0.0012 | +0.0077 |
| mid-network stream, off at 50% | +0.0080 | +0.0175 |
| final hidden, off at 20% | +0.0025 | |

**The byte-aux branch closes at d512.** The model learns the target's bytes readily (about 1.7 nats/byte), but that signal competes with the next-token loss rather than adding to it. At a 16k vocab, the lm_head input already carries the byte structure the next-token loss needs. This matches Parameter Golf's finding that auxiliary objectives hurt at a 2–5k-step horizon.

**Correction on the "V4.1" label:** our `mla_k_norm` normalizes each head's *up-projected* MLA key. DeepSeek V4.1 instead RMS-normalizes the shared KV latent, which is itself the key in their shared-KV MQA. The idea is related but not the same. Ours still works with MLA absorption at inference, at the cost of caching one inverse key norm per head per token (+0.8% KV cache at d512); see [this reply](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5860384921).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Understood: fewer sweeps, new ideas in depth, and several competing branches. The batch-67 re-tuning runs are already on the cluster, so I'll let them finish, and I won't queue further sweeps. How I'm organizing from here:

- **Every negative result gets a diagnosis from the learned behavior before it's dropped,** followed by at least one informed variant.
  - First example, the token-window source ([batch 65](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5858772158)): its AttnRes gate weight collapsed from uniform to about 0.005 within 350 steps, and its gradient fell about 20× with it. The gates starved it before it could become useful.
  - Variant now running: the window is summed into the token-embedding source, so it can't be gated away.
- **Parallel branches, each on candidate 2 and developed on its own:**
  1. **Local-context memory:** the token-window variants, then consumer-specific feeds (e.g. into the router or KDA q/k) if the summed form shows signal.
  2. **Heterogeneous experts:** two expert banks per layer (different widths or activations) under one router, with per-bank capacity so the bank FLOPs stay balanced. This is the next build.
  3. **Byte-level aux loss:** weight 0.1 was +0.0012. Its gradient was live until step ~1400 and 0 after, as designed. Next I'll add the byte loss to the logged metrics, check how far below ln 256 it gets, check how the byte head's features overlap the lm_head's, and then try tweaks like feeding the byte head from an earlier layer, or predicting the *current* token's bytes.
  4. **DeepSeek V4.1 attention items:** K-only norm is running; a learnable sink needs the FA4 bridge.

Each branch gets its own comment thread of results and diagnoses.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 68 (branch: heterogeneous experts): two expert banks per layer** (for [your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5858745269); d512, equal steps, on candidate 2 = 3.0197)

**Design** (`moe_bank2_*`, `c3b7085b34`):
- **Routing:** one router scores all `num_experts` experts; the last `moe_bank2_experts` of them form bank 2, with its own width and activation.
  - Each token takes a *fixed split*: `num_experts_per_token − moe_bank2_topk` from bank 1 and `moe_bank2_topk` from bank 2, top-k taken per bank on the biased logits.
  - Each bank's FLOPs are therefore fixed by construction, and the hardware sees two uniform-shape expert banks, each with its own pooled-wave dispatch.
- **Load balancing:** QB runs per bank. Each bank's threshold α is its own (k+1)-th biased logit, and its betas target that bank's own k/E. The betas are concatenated, so the QB bias state and train-step plumbing are unchanged.
- **Combine:** the weights are sigmoid, renormalized over all selected experts across both banks, so a token can put more weight on whichever bank serves it better.
- **CPU check (4-device EP mesh):** ReLU² + SwiGLU and ReLU² + ReLU² bank mixes train, bank 2 gets gradients, and the QB betas have shape `[layers, E_total]`. The single-bank path is unchanged.

**Three FLOPs-matched designs.** Candidate 2 is 384 ReLU² experts × width 384, top-8, i.e. 8 × 384 = 3072 expert-width units per token:
- **Widths:** 256 × width 256, top-6, plus 128 × width 768, top-2. That is 1536 + 1536 units: many specialists plus a few generalists.
- **Activations:** 192 ReLU² × 384, top-4, plus 192 SwiGLU × 256, top-4. Here SwiGLU's 3 GEMMs at 256 equal ReLU²'s 2 at 384.
- **One wide expert per token:** 384 × width 192, top-8, plus 64 × width 1536, top-1. That is 1536 + 1536 units: a near-dense wide path plus fine-grained experts.

The cost to watch is the second dispatch: two all-to-alls per layer instead of one. ex/s is reported per row. If a mix wins on loss but loses on speed, the next step is to fuse both banks into one dispatch with a per-bank column split.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| widths: 256×256 top-6 + 128×768 top-2 | [`bbeb97a670`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/bbeb97a670) | [lc1-b68-het-widths-r](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b68-het-widths-r) | 2817 | 739 | 3.2463 | 3.0207 | +0.0010 vs 3.0197 |
| activations: 192 ReLU²×384 top-4 + 192 SwiGLU×256 top-4 | [`c3b7085b34`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c3b7085b34) | [lc1-b68-het-act](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b68-het-act) | 2817 | 719 | 3.2501 | 3.0287 | +0.0090 vs 3.0197 |
| one wide: 384×192 top-8 + 64×1536 top-1 | [`bbeb97a670`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/bbeb97a670) | [lc1-b68-het-onewide-r](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b68-het-onewide-r) | 2817 | 700 | 3.2460 | 3.0253 | +0.0056 vs 3.0197 |

**Rerun (`-r`, `bbeb97a670`):** the widths design crashed at eval. The dropless eval swapped only the first expert bank's backend, so the ReLU² bank 2 stayed on its pooled-wave ungated setting and hit the local backend's tied-gate layout. Eval now swaps both banks. The activations design ran fine, because its bank 2 is gated SwiGLU.

**Activations mix: +0.0090.** The diagnosis will come with the other two designs, from per-bank expert norms and gradients.

**Diagnosing the activations mix (+0.0090).** Layer-0 learned norms:

| bank | weight Frobenius norm (hyperball-fixed) | ‖∇ w_up‖ | ‖∇ w_down‖ |
|---|---|---|---|
| ReLU² 192 × 384 | 94.7 | 0.0089 | 0.0096 |
| SwiGLU 192 × 256 | 77.3 | 0.0037 | 0.0061 |

- The SwiGLU bank trains with about 0.4–0.6× the gradient of the ReLU² bank.
- The two activations also give different output scales at the same input, and MuonH pins each bank's weight norm at init. The renormalized combine is shared across banks, so the router can't cheaply rebalance them.
- **There's a confound:** splitting 384 experts / top-8 into 2 × 192 at top-4 each is also a routing constraint, since a token can't pick all 8 experts from the kind it prefers.
- **Control queued:** the same fixed split with both banks ReLU² at width 384. It separates the cost of the forced split from the cost of SwiGLU.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| split control: 192 ReLU²×384 top-4 + 192 ReLU²×384 top-4 | [`bbeb97a670`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/bbeb97a670) | [lc1-b68-het-splitctl](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b68-het-splitctl) | 2817 | 725 | 3.2420 | 3.0197 | +0.0000 vs 3.0197 |

**Results and diagnosis:**

| design (FLOPs-matched to candidate 2) | Δ vs 3.0197 | ex/s |
|---|---|---|
| **split control:** 192 ReLU²×384 top-4 + 192 ReLU²×384 top-4 | **+0.0000** | 725 |
| widths: 256×256 top-6 + 128×768 top-2 | +0.0010 | **739** (candidate 2: 728) |
| one wide: 384×192 top-8 + 64×1536 top-1 | +0.0056 | 700 |
| activations: 192 ReLU²×384 top-4 + 192 SwiGLU×256 top-4 | +0.0090 | 719 |

- **The split itself is free.** Forcing each token to take 4 experts from each of two identical banks costs exactly nothing, so the fixed per-bank top-k and per-bank QB work. Every other delta comes from the banks' contents.
- **Mixing activations hurts** because of the imbalance measured above: the SwiGLU bank gets about half the gradient, and MuonH pins each bank's weight norm, so the banks' relative output magnitudes are frozen by their activations and widths.
- **One wide top-1 expert hurts:** a single coarse 64-expert bank is worse than fine-grained experts at the same FLOPs.
- **Widths are neutral on loss but about 1.5% faster** (739 vs 728 ex/s, within host noise). That would be worth about −0.0025 at fixed time if the speedup is real.
- **Informed tweak** (`71cbbc6901`): `moe_bank2_scale` adds a learnable output scale per bank (init 1, Adam), the degree of freedom MuonH takes away. It is tested on the activations mix, where the imbalance is largest, and on the widths mix.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| activations mix + per-bank scale | [`71cbbc6901`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/71cbbc6901) | [lc1-b68-het-act-scale](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b68-het-act-scale) | 2817 | 709 | 3.2476 | 3.0271 | +0.0074 vs 3.0197 |
| widths mix + per-bank scale | [`71cbbc6901`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/71cbbc6901) | [lc1-b68-het-widths-scale](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b68-het-widths-scale) | 2817 | 725 | 3.2430 | 3.0212 | +0.0015 vs 3.0197 |

**Per-bank scale: small recovery, no gain.** The activations mix goes from +0.0090 to **+0.0074**, and the widths mix is +0.0015 (vs +0.0010 without the scale).
- **The learned scales rebalance nothing.** Both banks' scales grow to about 2.3× in every layer (the 2-vector norms are about 3.1–3.6 across layers), in both mixes. The network wants a larger MoE output overall, not a different ratio between banks.
- That repeats batch 01's learned sublayer scales, where the MoE outputs grew to 1.2–2.1× and were neutral on loss. The imbalance in the activations mix is a *gradient* imbalance (the SwiGLU bank trains at about half the rate), and an output scale doesn't fix that.
- **The heterogeneous-experts branch closes at d512:** the split is free, but no bank mix beats uniform ReLU² 1.5×. The code (`moe_bank2_*`) stays in for hero-scale work, where per-bank widths could matter for hardware efficiency.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 69 (branch: local-context memory): an Engram-style content gate on the bigram source** (d512, equal steps, on candidate 2; seed 0 vs 3.0197, seed 1 vs 3.0266)

This comes from your trigram comment ("only propagate forward if I have property X and embed has property Y") and DeepSeek's Engram gate. AttnRes scores each source with a *static* pseudo-query, so a gate can depend on the bigram row itself but not on how the bigram row relates to the *current token*.

`bigram_gate` (`03ee1a03d5`) scales each token's bigram row by
`g_t = σ(Σ_d w_d · rms(e_t)_d · rms(b_t)_d + c)`,
an interaction between the token embedding `e_t` and its bigram row `b_t`.
- `w` starts at zero and `c` at +2, so the gate starts at a constant 0.88. Both are Adam parameters. Cost: one D-wide dot product per token.

🤖 **Batch 73 (branch: speed): shard the bigram table's optimizer state** (candidate 4, d512, equal steps; vs 3.0118 / 3.0166 at a 175.0 ms median step on 02a)

The bigram table is still the stack's biggest non-core cost: about 5% of step time at d512, worth about 0.0085 at fixed time. It is a replicated 524k × 512 parameter, so every step:
- every GPU runs Adam over all 268M table parameters (about 7 GB of HBM traffic for p, m, v and g, about 2 ms);

The math is identical (checked bit-exact on CPU in batch 53), so this measures pure step time.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 74 (branch: speed): where candidate 4's step goes, and overlapping the EP all-to-all** (d512, cw-us-east-02a)

A 100-step profile of candidate 4 (`lc1-b74-prof-c4`, 5 profiled steps on GPU 0; the per-step span is inflated to 163–170 ms by the profiler):

| | per step |
|---|---|
| compute | 141 ms |
| **exposed communication** | **18–26 ms** (11–15%) |
| idle / launch gaps | 2.4 ms |

**Top kernels:**
- NCCL SendRecv (the EP all-to-all): **26.3 ms**
- NCCL AllGather: 6.7 ms (the bigram-table lookup gather and the FSDP gathers)
- FA4 fwd + bwd: 3.9 + 3.2 ms
- KDA state fwd + bwd: 3.1 + 3.4 ms
- NCCL ReduceScatter: 2.6 ms

**The EP all-to-all is the largest remaining cost, and most of it is exposed.** Per GPU it moves 65k tokens × 8 assignments × the 256-wide latent in bf16, about 268 MB per all-to-all. With 4 per layer (dispatch and combine, forward and backward) over 6 layers, that's about 6.4 GB per step. At 0.0017 per 1% of step time, hiding all of the exposed part would be worth up to about **0.02** of loss at fixed time.

**First lever: waves** (`moe_expert_waves`, `d7bbf4ea14`).
- The pooled-wave backend already supports splitting the dispatch into static waves. Each wave's dispatch, expert compute and combine are independent of the others, so XLA's latency-hiding scheduler can run wave k+1's all-to-all under wave k's expert GEMMs.
- Our init hard-coded 1 wave; these profiles test 2 and 4. The cost is more, smaller all-to-alls (more per-message latency) and a finer per-wave capacity.
- If the overlap shows up in the profile, full runs will check that loss is unchanged: the capacity per wave is the same fraction of assignments.

|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 141 ms | 18–26 ms (mean 23.0) | 172.8 ms |
| 2 | 143 ms | 17–26 ms (mean 19.9) | 171.0 ms (−1%) |
| 4 | 148 ms | 19–20 ms (mean 19.6) | 179.1 ms (+4%) |

- Two waves hide about 3 ms of the all-to-all and add about 2 ms of compute; four waves add 7 ms of compute for no more overlap.
- XLA is barely overlapping the all-to-all with the other wave's expert GEMMs, even though the waves are independent and the latency-hiding scheduler is on.
- The grug d6144 work found the same failure mode: the scheduler made the wrong overlap calls with its *heuristic* collective latencies, and **PGLE** (profile-guided latency estimation, which recompiles with measured latencies) gave +1.1–1.3 pt MFU there.

**Next:** `--pgle-runs 5` (`646eae2511`) sets `jax_enable_pgle` / `jax_pgle_profiling_runs` through the trainer's jax_config: it profiles 5 steps, then recompiles once. Two full runs on candidate 4: PGLE alone, and PGLE with 2 waves, where measured latencies may let the scheduler actually overlap the waves.

**Consolidated run:** every adopted win is now one config, candidate 4 with the sharded table. It is launched on 2 seeds as `lc1-cand4-s0` / `lc1-cand4-s1` (`646eae2511`), with the exact flag list in the rewritten **Status → Current best recipe**. The Status section now has three parts: the current recipe, a numbered table of adopted wins in order with paired Δ / step cost / running result, and the scale checks. The out-of-order candidate rows are gone.

**Key-only norm and MLA absorption.** First, a correction: our `mla_k_norm` is *not* DeepSeek V4.1's setup, and I've fixed the label.
- **V4.1** RMS-normalizes the shared KV latent, which is itself the key (shared-KV MQA, no up-projection). That is trivially cache-compatible.
- **Ours** normalizes each head's *up-projected* key: `k_h = W_uk,h · c` → `k_h / ‖k_h‖`.

It still absorbs, with one extra scalar per head per cached token:
- **Score:** absorbed MLA computes `q_h · k_h = (W_uk,hᵀ q_h) · c = q̃_h · c`. With the norm, the score is `(q̃_h · c_j) · r_{j,h}`, where `r_{j,h} = 1/‖W_uk,h c_j‖` depends only on key position j.
- **With our partial key offset:** `k = [W^A c_{j−1}; W^B c_j]`, so `r_{j,h} = (‖W^A_h c_{j−1}‖² + ‖W^B_h c_j‖²)^(−½)`, still a function of the cache alone.
- **Cost:** compute `r` when a token enters the cache and store it next to the latent: n_heads floats per token (4 at d512, beside a 512-dim latent). At decode the kernel multiplies each key's score by its `r`. No up-projection is materialized, and the KV cache grows by 4 / 512 ≈ 0.8%.

**Q-norm** would also be absorption-friendly, since it only rescales the query, which is computed fresh at decode. It was the *combination* QK-norm that didn't fit our MLA training.

**Answers to your three questions:**
- **Normalize q too?** Yes, and it's free. Under MLA absorption each query is recomputed per token and never cached, so a weightless per-head query RMSNorm (`mla_q_norm`) costs no cache at any head count. Only the key side has a cache cost, and the shared key norm above cuts that to 1 float per token. So the hero-scale option would be a per-head query norm plus a shared key norm. The rows above test q+k with both the per-head and the shared key norm.
- **qk_mult init.** You're right that 2.5 is low. With the key norm on, the learned qk_mult in both MLA layers jumps from 2.5 to ~3.1 in the first 200 steps, then keeps climbing to 3.59 at the end, the same in both seeds. It was still rising when training stopped. With the query also normed, qk_mult carries all of the logit temperature, so I'd expect it to want even more. The rows above test init 4.0 with and without the query norm.
- **The 8-minute budget.** Candidate 4 is about 3% over. The median step is 175 ms, so 2817 steps × 175 ms ≈ 493 s. That's 8.2 min against 480 s, about 2.8% over; summed step time excluding compile is about 3.6% over. The exchange rate (0.0017 loss per 1% of step time) puts it at about +0.005 at equal time. Rather than rely on that projection, the last two rows run candidate 4 at 2740 steps, which fits in 480 s. The PGLE runs from batch 74 are still going and could recover part of the gap.

**Batch 75 results** (final Paloma macro loss; each Δ is paired against candidate 4 on the same seed, 3.0129 / 3.0161)

| variant | extra cached floats / token at hero scale | mean Δ | learned qk_mult (MLA L3 / L5) |
|---|---|---|---|
| per-head key norm (candidate 4) | n_heads | 0 | 3.6 / 3.6 (init 2.5, still rising) |
| shared key norm | 1 | +0.0037 | 3.5 / 3.5 |
| q norm + per-head key norm | n_heads | −0.0010 | 2.3 / 1.9 |
| q norm + shared key norm | 1 | +0.0023 | 2.1 / 1.8 |
| per-head key norm, qk_mult init 4 | n_heads | −0.0015 (seeds split) | 4.8 / 4.6 (still rising) |
| **q norm + per-head key norm, qk_mult init 4** | n_heads | **−0.0026 (both seeds)** | 3.1 / 2.9 |
| candidate 4 at 2740 steps (inside 480 s) | | +0.0058 | |

- **The shared key norm loses most of the gain.** It keeps about a third of the per-head norm's −0.0056. Adding the query norm doesn't bring it back. So the benefit seems to come from equalizing key magnitude *per head*, and one RMS across heads doesn't do that. At hero scale, the choice is n_heads cached floats per token or giving up most of the gain.
- **The query norm helps only with a higher qk_mult init.** Normalizing q removes q's own magnitude, so qk_mult carries all of the logit temperature. From init 2.5 it drifts *down* to about 2 and the result is neutral. From init 4 it settles near 3 and both seeds improve by 0.0026.
- **qk_mult isn't LR-starved late in training.** From step 20 to 150 it moves ~0.004 per step, close to Adam's maximum. After step 1200 it moves ~0.0001 per step, far below the rate the LR allows. So the endpoint is a basin that depends on the init, not an unconverged value. With the key norm alone it is still rising at the end, from both inits.
- **Budget:** at 2740 steps, candidate 4 fits in 480 s and loses +0.0058. The fixed-time exchange rate predicted +0.0048, so that rate is roughly right. PGLE (batch 74) makes up most of this gap; see batch 76.

🤖 **Batch 77: a wide sweep of new papers** (d512, equal steps, 2 seeds each)

H100s are plentiful, so this batch tests nine new ideas at once, each behind a default-off flag. The base is **candidate 5 without PGLE**: candidate 4 + MLA query norm + qk_mult init 4 (3.0103 / 3.0135 in batch 75). PGLE is left out until the step-2560 crash is understood (batch 76). The base is rerun here on the same commit, so every idea is paired against a same-batch reference.

| idea | paper | what it changes |
|---|---|---|
| Polar Express NS | arXiv 2505.16932 | MuonH Newton–Schulz coefficients tuned per iteration (`coefficient_type=polar_express`) |
| AOL NS | Turbo-Muon | AOL-preconditioned Newton–Schulz (`coefficient_type=aol`) |
| AdEMAMix | arXiv 2409.03152 | Adam groups (incl. the embedding tables) add a slow gradient EMA, α=5, β3=0.999, both warmed up over the run |
| Grokfast-EMA | arXiv 2405.20233 | every gradient gets 2× its EMA (α=0.98) added before the optimizer |
| DyT | arXiv 2503.10622 | block pre-RMSNorms → γ·tanh(αx)+β (α init 0.8 attention / 0.2 MLP) |
| Per-layer embeddings | Gemma 3n PLE | a 64-dim token table per layer, gated by the hidden state and added to each attention input; zero-init up-projection |
| Differential attention | arXiv 2410.05258 | MLA layers: softmax(q1k1) − λ·softmax(q2k2), with a second q and key up-projection (same head_dim) |

**First results.**
- **Polar Express is neutral**: +0.0003 / +0.0021 against the base. The likely reason is MuonH itself: the hyperball renormalizes every update, so a more accurate polar factor changes little. NS is also a small share of the step here, so a 4-step Polar Express would save little time.
- **AOL diverged (loss 5.2), and the cause is our implementation, not the idea.** AOL's coefficients (Turbo-Muon) are a 4-step schedule for inputs preconditioned by AOL column rescaling (D^-1/2 with D_ii = Σ_j|XXᵀ|_ij). Our Newton–Schulz only Frobenius-normalizes, and with `backend_steps=5` it wraps back to the first coefficient triple. That triple's polynomial at σ=1 is 4.0098 − 7.0585 + 2.4635 = −0.585, so every converged singular value gets flipped. The proper Turbo-Muon implementation (AOL preconditioner reusing the first Gram matrix, exactly 4 iterations) is in progress and will be rerun.
- **Per-head qk_mult** (new row) follows from batch 75. The per-head key norm helped by equalizing each head's logit scale, so this lets each head learn its own temperature.

**DyT:** both runs hung at the step-1407 dropless eval, for over 50 minutes: the eval loader was waiting on 64 items. Every other run launched at the same time finished normally. They were cancelled and resubmitted as `-r`. If they hang again, it's something about the DyT model at eval.

comments.body: Most of these ideas should not be ruled out after one failed test. Requires thinking about how to tune each and looking at how it’s interacting with the model.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Agreed. For batch 77 I'm treating every idea as a branch, not a single test. Each one's learned knobs are now logged per layer as `train/attn_res/knob_*` (`fdef2f88b4`). I resubmitted the four runs that have those knobs so the first results come with them:

- **value residual:** λ1 / λ2
- **differential attention:** effective λ
- **DyT:** α
- **per-layer embeddings:** up-projection norm
- **MoE++:** null-slot fraction per layer

Each gets a second round tuned from what the model actually does with it. For example: whether value residual takes up layer 0's values or pushes λ2 to zero, and whether DyT's α drifts away from its init. That round is then run on its own merits, rather than rejecting the idea after one run.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 78: second iterations, tuned from what batch 77's runs learned** (d512, paired against `lc1-b77-base5`: 3.0099 / 3.0139)

**AdEMAMix wins early and gives it back.** Final loss is +0.0023 / +0.0022, but the paired train-loss gap (50-step smoothed) shows the whole picture, and it is the same on both seeds:

| step | 200 | 500 | 1000 | 1500 | 2000 | 2400 | 2810 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AdEMAMix − base | −0.032 | −0.036 | −0.024 | −0.012 | −0.007 | −0.002 | ±0.000 |

At step 500 that is a large speedup: the slow gradient EMA helps the Adam groups early, and those include both embedding tables, whose rows update sparsely. The lead fades as α ramps toward 5 while the LR decays. A slow momentum with a ~1000-step horizon carries stale directions into the final convergence. Two tuned versions:
- **Warm up, then cool down:** α reaches 5 by 10% of the run, holds, then decays to 0 over the last 30%, so the tail is plain Adam.
- **Shorter slow horizon:** β3 = 0.99 (~100 steps) with the paper's schedule.

**Grokfast (λ=2, every group) is worse throughout:** +0.045 to +0.09 in train loss from step 200, and +0.042 final. On MuonH, adding a gradient EMA before the momentum is effectively a higher momentum. Batch 7 already found MuonH momentum 0.98 costs +0.034, so this is the same failure. Tuned version: Adam groups only, λ=1.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Turbo-Muon, reimplemented** (arXiv 2512.04632). The first Gram matrix A = XXᵀ is formed from the raw X. X is rescaled by s = rsqrt(Σ_j|A_ij|) and A by s_i s_j, so the rescaled Gram costs no extra matmul. Then exactly 4 iterations run with the paper's coefficients: the last four quintic triples. Levanter's old `aol` table was an early draft from the reference repo.

Singular values after orthogonalization, vs the exact polar factor (bf16):

| input | quintic ×5 | polar_express ×5 | AOL ×4 (fixed) | old AOL (Frobenius, 5 cyclic steps) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512×1536 Gaussian: σ min/max, err | 0.985/1.055, 0.025 | 0.808/1.129, 0.097 | 0.987/1.062, 0.033 | 0.499/0.971, **1.64** |
| 512×1536, σ_i∝i^-1 | 0.687/1.153, 0.145 | 0.816/1.131, 0.107 | 0.211/1.152, 0.478 | 0.007/1.204, 0.68 |

- The old error of 1.64 means directions were sign-flipped, which explains the divergence.
- The fix matches quintic with one fewer iteration, except on steeply decaying spectra, where AOL's row-sum bound over-shrinks.
- Polar Express at 5 steps (the first 5 of an 8-step schedule) is far from converged: σ ranges 0.80–1.13. That is a second reason it was neutral.

**MoE++ (batch 77): the router mostly avoids the null experts.**
- **Free split:** only 0.9% / 1.7% of top-8 slots go to null experts, almost all of them zero experts; copy and constant go unused. The loss is within noise: +0.0025 / +0.0013.
- **QB-forced 25% null share:** it spreads evenly over layers (≈12% zero, 7% copy, 7% constant) and costs +0.015. That is the price of about 6 real experts per token. So far this saves no compute, since null slots still ride the fixed-capacity dispatch.

The question MoE++ really asks is whether routing some tokens to nothing beats a plain top-6 at the same average compute. The control is below. It also measures the step time top-6 would buy once null slots skip dispatch.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |

| top-6 routed experts (control for MoE++ 25% null) | [`a9557bfa07`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a9557bfa07) | [lc1-b78-top6](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b78-top6) | 2817 | 789 | 3.2377 | 3.0141 | +0.0042 vs 3.0099 |
| same, seed 1 | [`a9557bfa07`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a9557bfa07) | [lc1-b78-top6-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b78-top6-s1) | 2817 | 796 | 3.2425 | 3.0178 | +0.0039 vs 3.0139 |

**What the batch 77 architecture ideas learned** (paired Δ vs base 3.0099 / 3.0139; knobs are end-of-run values)

- **Value residual: used heavily, but no loss gain** (all layers −0.0017 / 0.0000; MLA only +0.0002 / +0.0001).
  - The KDA layers switch it off: λ2 is 0.02–0.13 against λ1 ≈ 0.5.
  - Both MLA layers lean on layer 0's values: L3 has λ2 1.0–1.3 vs λ1 0.7. **L5 has λ2 ≈ 3.0 vs λ1 ≈ 0.3**, so its values are mostly layer 0's. This holds on both seeds and in both variants.
  - So the last softmax layer wants early, near-token-identity values. Block AttnRes already provides an equivalent path to early representations, which is why using it changes nothing. Closed, with this finding noted for AttnRes.
- **Differential attention: the model turns subtraction into addition.**
  - Learned λ is negative in 3 of 4 layer-seeds (−1.68, −0.93, −1.52; one +0.77), so out ≈ a₁ + |λ|·a₂. That's two attention maps summed, i.e. extra attention capacity, not noise cancellation.
  - Loss is −0.0016, but the step takes 186 ms vs 175 (+6%, two kernel calls on 2 layers), worth ≈+0.011 at fixed time. Closed: the noise DIFF cancels doesn't seem to exist in our two q/k-normed global MLA layers.
- **Per-layer embeddings: under-trained early, then unstable, from a too-hot LR.**
  - Seed 1 trails the base from the start (train loss 2.987 vs 2.882 at step 200) and takes a +0.31 spike at step 2240. It ends +0.059. Seed 0 also starts slower, then catches up (+0.0014).
  - Its up-projection norms grow to 11–22, twice seed 0's.
  - Cause: the 49M-row PLE table inherited `embed2_lr_mult=10`, the 10× Adam LR meant for the bigram table. It now has its own group (`ple_lr_mult`, `405a2080b8`), rerun at 1× and 3×.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLE 64, table at 1× Adam LR | [`405a2080b8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/405a2080b8) | [lc1-b78-ple64-lr1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b78-ple64-lr1) | 2817 | 727 | 3.2386 | 3.0100 | +0.0001 vs 3.0099 |

| PLE 64, table at 3× Adam LR | [`405a2080b8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/405a2080b8) | [lc1-b78-ple64-lr3](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b78-ple64-lr3) | 2817 | 712 | 3.3023 | 3.0748 | +0.0649 vs 3.0099 |

**Per-head qk_mult (batch 77) is neutral: −0.0001 / +0.0011.** The heads end close together: L3 2.8–3.3 (mean 3.1), L5 2.4–3.0 (mean 2.8), on both seeds. Those means match the per-layer scalar's endpoints (3.1 / 2.9). So with q and k normed, the heads don't want different temperatures, and the per-layer scalar is enough. The per-head *key norm* gain therefore comes from normalizing each head's per-token key magnitude, not from per-head temperature. Closed.

**AdEMAMix, round 2** (paired train-loss gap vs base, 50-step smoothed)

| variant | 200 | 500 | 1000 | 1500 | 2000 | 2400 | 2810 | final |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| round 1: α 5, β3 0.999, paper warmup over the run | −0.032 | −0.036 | −0.024 | −0.012 | −0.007 | −0.002 | ±0.000 | +0.0023 |
| α 5 by 10%, cooldown over last 30% | +0.033 | +0.133 | +0.289 | +0.325 | +0.265 | +0.437 | +0.413 | **3.43 (unstable)** |
| **β3 0.99, paper warmup** | −0.026 | −0.019 | −0.008 | −0.001 | +0.001 | +0.001 | −0.003 | **−0.0024** (seed 0) |

- **Fast warmup diverges on both seeds.** The paper's slow joint warmup of α and β3 is load-bearing, not cosmetic: full α on a still-short slow EMA destabilizes the embedding tables within 500 steps.
- **A shorter slow horizon keeps the early lead without the late fade.** With β3 = 0.99 (~100 steps), the early lead is a bit smaller, but the gap doesn't turn positive during the LR decay, and the run ends ahead. That fits the round-1 diagnosis: a slow EMA with a ~1000-step horizon carries stale directions into the decay. Seed 1 is running. Next: bracket β3 at 0.98 / 0.995.

It becomes a candidate-6 component, pending the β3 bracket above.

Grokfast on the Adam groups only (λ 1), seed 1: **+0.0071** (3.0210 vs 3.0139). Taking it off MuonH removed the blow-up but not the harm. Seed 0 is still rerunning after two node failures.

**Per-layer embeddings, round 2: the table LR is not the cause. The runs are bimodal.**

| PLE table LR | seed 0 | seed 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 10× (batch 77) | 3.0113 (up norms 7–10) | 3.0726 (up norms 11–22) |
| 1× | 3.0100 (7–10) | 3.0730 (12–24) |
| 3× | 3.0748 (11–21) | 3.0728 (12–23) |

- Each run lands in one of two modes: base level (≈3.010, up-projection norms ~7–10) or a bad mode (≈3.073, norms ~12–24, behind from step 200). LR changes which mode seed 0 lands in, not where the modes sit.
- The +0.4 train-loss "spike" at step ~2240 appears in non-PLE runs too (Grokfast has it), so it's a data artifact, not instability.
- Likely mechanism: every token's PLE row is RMS-normalized before gating, so even an untrained table injects fixed-size noise into every attention input once the Adam-trained up-projection grows. Some seeds lock into using it.
- **Closed.** Even the good mode only matches the base (−0.0001 / +0.0014), so no upside is left to stabilize: the bigram table + AttnRes already covers what per-layer token tables give.

**Grokfast on the Adam groups only: +0.0071 / +0.0071** (3.0170 / 3.0210). Closed. Neither the Muon groups (extra momentum) nor the Adam groups (embeddings) benefit from amplifying the slow gradient component this way. AdEMAMix, which mixes a slow EMA into Adam's first moment rather than into the gradient, is what works.

| 0.99 (~100) | −0.0024 | −0.0045 | −0.0035 |
| 0.995 (~200) | −0.0031 | −0.0028 | −0.0030 |
| 0.999 (~1000, batch 77) | +0.0023 | +0.0022 | +0.0023 |

The optimum sits at the short end, so the bracket continues below 0.98, and α 8 is tried at 0.98.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AdEMAMix α 5, β3 0.95 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b78-ademamix-b95](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b78-ademamix-b95) | 2817 | 719 | 3.2408 | 3.0061 | −0.0038 vs 3.0099 |
| same, seed 1 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b78-ademamix-b95-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b78-ademamix-b95-s1) | 2817 | 729 | 3.2480 | 3.0103 | −0.0036 vs 3.0139 |
| AdEMAMix α 8, β3 0.98 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b78-ademamix-b98-a8](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b78-ademamix-b98-a8) | 2817 | 724 | 3.2398 | 3.0090 | −0.0009 vs 3.0099 |
| same, seed 1 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b78-ademamix-b98-a8-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b78-ademamix-b98-a8-s1) | 2817 | 730 | 3.2474 | 3.0128 | −0.0011 vs 3.0139 |

**β3 0.95: −0.0038 / −0.0036 (mean −0.0037).** With 0.98 at −0.0041, 0.99 at −0.0035 and 0.995 at −0.0030, the optimum is a broad plateau over 0.95–0.99. **AdEMAMix α 5, β3 0.98 goes into candidate 6.** α 8 is still running.

**α 8 at β3 0.98 is worse than α 5: −0.0009 / −0.0011** (vs −0.0051 / −0.0031 for α 5). A heavier slow EMA gives back most of the gain, so α 5 stays.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 79: fewer experts per token, and removing EP recompute** (d512, paired vs base 3.0099 / 3.0139 at 175.0 / 176.2 ms)

**What came in**

| run | Δ at equal steps | median step | at fixed time (0.0017 per 1%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **top-6 routed experts** (vs top-8) | +0.0042 / +0.0039 | **162.2 / 160.7 ms (−8.0%)** | **≈ −0.010** |
| MoE++ with a forced 25% null share | +0.0070 / +0.0155 | no change | +0.011 |
| Turbo-Muon (AOL, fixed), 4 NS steps | +0.0029 / +0.0022 | 176.4 / 171.8 ms | ≈ +0.002 |
| FP8 dispatch (first 1400 steps, then the eval crash) | train loss identical | 175.1 / 178.2 ms (no change) | 0 |

- **Top-6 is the biggest fixed-time lever found in a while.** It costs +0.004 at equal steps, but steps are 8% faster.
  - We never measured top-k at fixed time on the current recipe.
  - It also closes MoE++: dropping experts uniformly (+0.004) beats learned null routing at a similar 25% cut (+0.011).
  - Below: top-6 at its in-budget step count (480 s / 161.5 ms ≈ 2972 steps), plus top-5 and top-4 at equal steps to find the knee.
- **Turbo-Muon loses to quintic** despite correct preconditioning. Our momentum matrices likely have the steep spectra where AOL's row-sum bound over-shrinks. Closed.
- **FP8 dispatch saves no time.** Quantize/dequantize eats the ~1–3 ms from halving 1 of the 5 same-size all-to-alls per wave. Closed. It crashed at eval because the dropless eval's `sonic` backend rejected the flag; fixed in `9dcd6fc2ec`.

**New systems ideas, both aimed at the 18–26 ms of exposed EP time**
- **No expert recompute** (`moe_expert_remat=false`, `2b98a02534`). The FP8 analysis found that every wave's expert MLP and combine all-to-all run under `jax.checkpoint(nothing_saveable)`. So the backward repeats the expert up/down GEMMs and one full all-to-all per wave, i.e. 1 of 5 collectives is pure recompute. d512 peaks at ~34.5 GiB of 80, so there's room to save those instead.
- **Shortcut-connected MoE** (ScMoE, arXiv 2404.05019 / LongCat-Flash 2509.01322; `moe_shortcut=true`). Layer l's MoE gate mixes the same AttnRes sources layer l's attention saw, with its own pseudo-query. So the MoE input no longer depends on the same layer's attention output: a JVP check gives exactly zero for ∂MoE_l/∂attn_l, while attn_l still reaches every later gate. The dispatch all-to-all can then overlap that layer's attention. This is also an ML change, since the MoE loses one source.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **top-6, fixed time** (2972 steps ≈ 480 s) | [`9dcd6fc2ec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/9dcd6fc2ec) | [lc1-b79-top6-ft](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-top6-ft) | 2972 | 786 | 3.2337 | 3.0059 | −0.0040 vs 3.0099 |
| same, seed 1 | [`9dcd6fc2ec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/9dcd6fc2ec) | [lc1-b79-top6-ft-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-top6-ft-s1) | 2972 | 794 | 3.2369 | 3.0109 | −0.0030 vs 3.0139 |
| top-5, equal steps | [`9dcd6fc2ec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/9dcd6fc2ec) | [lc1-b79-top5](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-top5) | 2817 | 825 | 3.2398 | 3.0178 | +0.0079 vs 3.0099 |
| same, seed 1 | [`9dcd6fc2ec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/9dcd6fc2ec) | [lc1-b79-top5-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-top5-s1) | 2817 | 818 | 3.2503 | 3.0233 | +0.0094 vs 3.0139 |
| top-4, equal steps | [`9dcd6fc2ec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/9dcd6fc2ec) | [lc1-b79-top4](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-top4) | 2817 | 845 | 3.2476 | 3.0251 | +0.0152 vs 3.0099 |
| same, seed 1 | [`9dcd6fc2ec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/9dcd6fc2ec) | [lc1-b79-top4-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-top4-s1) | 2817 | 864 | 3.2553 | 3.0281 | +0.0142 vs 3.0139 |
| no expert recompute | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b79-noremat](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-noremat) | 2817 | 725 | 3.2366 | 3.0095 | −0.0004 vs 3.0099 |
| same, seed 1 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b79-noremat-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-noremat-s1) | 2817 | 722 | 3.2397 | 3.0145 | +0.0006 vs 3.0139 |
| ScMoE shortcut | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b79-scmoe](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-scmoe) | 2817 | | | running | vs 3.0099 |

| ScMoE + no expert recompute | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b79-scmoe-noremat](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-scmoe-noremat) | 2817 | | | running | vs 3.0099 |
| same, seed 1 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b79-scmoe-noremat-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-scmoe-noremat-s1) | 2817 | | | running | vs 3.0139 |

**Top-k scan** (paired vs base 3.0099 / 3.0139 at ~175.6 ms; fixed-time projection uses 0.0017 per 1% of step time)

| routed top-k | Δ at equal steps | median step | at fixed time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 (base) | 0 | 175.6 ms | 0, but 2817 steps ≈ 493 s is over budget |
| 6, run at 2972 steps (≈484 s) | **−0.0040 / −0.0030** (measured vs the 2817-step base) | 162.0 ms (−7.8%) | ≈ −0.009 vs an in-budget top-8 |
| 5 | +0.0079 / +0.0094 | 155.8 ms (−11.3%) | ≈ −0.0105 (projected) |
| 4 | +0.0152 / +0.0142 | 149.9 ms (−14.6%) | ≈ −0.0102 (projected) |

- **The fixed-time gain is flat from top-6 to top-4, about −0.010 each.** For changes this large the linear exchange rate is only a guide, so below: top-5 and top-4 at their in-budget step counts, plus an in-budget top-8 (2740 steps) for a direct fixed-time comparison.
- **Caveat for the 1e24 projection:** top-k trades FLOPs per token for quality, and the fixed-time optimum at d512 depends on d512's comm/compute ratio. The scale checks must use the scaling-law (compute-multiplier) view, not the d512 step-time gain.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| top-8 base, in budget | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b79-base-ft](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-base-ft) | 2740 | 739 | 3.2434 | 3.0169 | +0.0070 vs 3.0099 |
| same, seed 1 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b79-base-ft-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-base-ft-s1) | 2740 | 728 | 3.2442 | 3.0190 | +0.0051 vs 3.0139 |
| top-5, in budget | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b79-top5-ft](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-top5-ft) | 3080 | 810 | 3.2243 | 3.0046 | vs lc1-b79-base-ft |
| same, seed 1 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b79-top5-ft-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-top5-ft-s1) | 3080 | 816 | 3.2287 | 3.0085 | vs lc1-b79-base-ft-s1 |
| top-4, in budget | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b79-top4-ft](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-top4-ft) | 3200 | 843 | 3.2293 | 3.0062 | vs lc1-b79-base-ft |
| same, seed 1 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b79-top4-ft-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b79-top4-ft-s1) | 3200 | 852 | 3.2294 | 3.0036 | vs lc1-b79-base-ft-s1 |

**No expert recompute does nothing:** 3.0095 / 3.0145, at 176.6 / 177.1 ms and 34.6 GiB peak. Loss, step time and memory all match the base. So the pooled-wave backend's inner `jax.checkpoint` isn't the operative remat: the layer-level AttnRes backward already decides what gets saved, and XLA treats the inner checkpoint as a no-op. Closed.

**Top-k at fixed time, measured directly** (paired vs the in-budget top-8 base: 2740 steps, 3.0169 / 3.0190)

| routed top-k | steps | time | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 2740 | 475 / 482 s | 3.0169 | 3.0190 | 0 |
| 6 | 2972 | 484 / 479 s | −0.0110 | −0.0081 | **−0.0096** |
| 5 | 3080 | 486 / 483 s | −0.0123 | −0.0105 | **−0.0114** |
| 4 | 3200 | 486 / 481 s | −0.0107 | −0.0154 | **−0.0131** |

The gain is a plateau of −0.010 to −0.013 from top-6 to top-4. The differences between them are within seed noise, and the linear exchange-rate projections were accurate. The in-budget top-8 base also confirms the budget cost: 2740 steps is +0.0055 worse than the over-budget 2817 steps.

Candidate 6 is in batch 80: candidate 5 without PGLE, plus AdEMAMix (α 5, β3 0.98), plus top-6 / 5 / 4 at step counts that fit strictly inside 480 s. Before any top-k choice goes further, it gets a scale check, since fewer routed FLOPs per token is exactly the kind of change whose value shifts with scale.

**ScMoE shortcut: +0.038 for a 1.7% faster step** (seed 1: 3.0519 vs 3.0139; 173.2 vs 176.2 ms). The MoE of each layer needs that layer's attention output. Losing it costs roughly 10× what the attention/dispatch overlap buys (≈ −0.003 at the fixed-time rate). The seed-0 and shortcut+no-recompute runs hung for over an hour in a CuTeDSL kernel compile (a cache miss) before step 0, so they were cancelled rather than rerun: the direction is clear from seed 1, and no-recompute was already shown to be a no-op. Closed.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 80: candidate 6** (d512, **in-budget step counts**, paired vs the in-budget top-8 base `lc1-b79-base-ft`: 3.0169 / 3.0190)

Candidate 6 = candidate 5 without PGLE (candidate 4 + MLA query norm + qk_mult init 4) plus two new wins:
- **AdEMAMix on the Adam groups**, α 5 and β3 0.98 with the paper's warmup (batch 78: −0.0041 at equal steps, step time unchanged).
- **Fewer routed experts per token** (batch 79: −0.010 to −0.013 at fixed time for top-6 / 5 / 4).

Each variant's step count is trimmed so it finishes inside 480 s of train-step time. PGLE stays out until it has more clean runs; it would add another ~2.3%.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| candidate 6, top-6 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b80-c6-top6](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b80-c6-top6) | 2950 | 790 | 3.2368 | 3.0026 | −0.0143 vs 3.0169 |
| same, seed 1 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b80-c6-top6-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b80-c6-top6-s1) | 2950 | 779 | 3.2374 | 3.0063 | −0.0127 vs 3.0190 |
| candidate 6, top-5 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b80-c6-top5](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b80-c6-top5) | 3050 | 817 | 3.2299 | 3.0036 | −0.0133 vs 3.0169 |
| same, seed 1 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b80-c6-top5-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b80-c6-top5-s1) | 3050 | 808 | 3.2394 | 3.0090 | −0.0100 vs 3.0190 |
| candidate 6, top-4 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b80-c6-top4](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b80-c6-top4) | 3170 | 861 | 3.2390 | 3.0029 | −0.0140 vs 3.0169 |
| same, seed 1 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b80-c6-top4-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b80-c6-top4-s1) | 3170 | 864 | 3.2363 | 3.0046 | −0.0144 vs 3.0190 |

**DyT (batch 77, resubmitted runs): +0.0154 / +0.0154, ~1% slower.** The learned α values show why (init → end of run):
- **MLP inputs:** 0.2 → **1.9–3.0** in every layer, both seeds.
- **Attention inputs:** 0.8 → 1.0–1.45 in the KDA layers, but 0.68–0.79 in the two MLA layers.

The paper's inits come from LLaMA-7B, and its own width study says narrower models need a larger α. So at d512 the run spent its training growing α up to a workable value. Second round: init α at the learned values (attention 1.2, MLP 2.2).

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DyT, α init 1.2 attention / 2.2 MLP | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b80-dyt-a](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b80-dyt-a) | 2817 | 719 | 3.2524 | 3.0246 | +0.0147 vs 3.0099 |
| same, seed 1 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b80-dyt-a-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b80-dyt-a-s1) | 2817 | 721 | 3.2566 | 3.0306 | +0.0167 vs 3.0139 |

**Candidate 6 results** (fixed time; Δ paired vs the in-budget top-8 base 3.0169 / 3.0190)

| routed top-k | steps | train-step time | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 2950 | 478 / 484 s | 3.0026 | 3.0063 | −0.0135 |
| 5 | 3050 | 478 / 483 s | 3.0036 | 3.0090 | −0.0117 |
| **4** | 3170 | **471 / 469 s** | **3.0029** | **3.0046** | **−0.0142** |

- Against in-budget candidate 4 (3.0183 / 3.0223, batch 75), that's ≈ **−0.016 at fixed time**.
- By the scaling-law formula this is k ≈ 2.1× vs clean KMA and 1.46× vs soft-cap 10. The Status section now lists candidate 6 (top-4) as the current best.
- The three top-k settings are within noise of each other. Top-4 still has 9–11 s of budget left (≈60 more steps).

**Scale check before adopting a top-k for the projection.** Fewer routed FLOPs per token is exactly the kind of change whose value can shift with scale. First step: d768 at the baseline step count (7325), top-8 vs top-4. That gives the equal-step loss cost of top-4 at d768 and the step-time saving there, to compare in k-space against d512.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 candidate 6 recipe, top-8 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b80-d768-c6-top8](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b80-d768-c6-top8) | 7325 | 324 | 2.9758 | 2.7689 | −0.0545 vs 2.8234 |
| d768 candidate 6 recipe, top-4 | [`b777db357b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b777db357b) | [lc1-b80-d768-c6-top4](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b80-d768-c6-top4) | 7325 | 393 | 2.9822 | 2.7816 | vs lc1-b80-d768-c6-top8 |

**DyT, round 2 (α init 1.2 attention / 2.2 MLP): +0.0147 / +0.0167**, no better than round 1 (+0.0154 / +0.0154). α keeps climbing from the higher init too: MLP 2.2 → 2.8–3.4, attention 1.2 → 1.2–1.7 (the MLA layers stay lowest at 0.9–1.0). So the init was never the problem: the model uses DyT as a gain, not as a squashing. The steady ~0.015 gap is the cost of losing per-token RMS normalization. That matters here because Block AttnRes mixes sources of very different magnitudes into each sublayer input. Closed.

🤖 **Batch 81: building on candidate 6** (d512, fixed time; paired vs candidate 6 top-4 at 3170 steps, 3.0029 / 3.0046, with a same-commit rerun as reference)

- **Spend the leftover budget.** Candidate 6 finishes in 469–471 s. With PGLE (−2.3% step time in batch 76, now with the eval fix), 3230 steps should still fit.
- **Top-3.** Top-6, 5 and 4 were flat at fixed time. At ~141 ms, top-3 would get ~3380 steps. Does the plateau continue?
- **Put compute back where top-4 took it away,** at top-4's step count, so their step-time cost shows up directly: wider routed experts (512 vs 384), or a wider shared expert (768 vs 384).
- **EP capacity factors 1.15 → 1.0.** With top-4 the dispatch is smaller; this measures the step time saved against extra drops.
- **Elementwise gated attention** (arXiv 2505.06708's best variant G1, `attn_gate_elementwise`, `5b99f0f772`): the MLA output gate becomes per channel (2σ(xW_g), W_g [D, N·H], zero-init) instead of one scalar per head.
- A product-key memory layer (Memory Layers at Scale, arXiv 2412.09764) is being implemented and will join.

**Product-key memory layer** (Memory Layers at Scale, arXiv 2412.09764; `memory_layers`, `061c01cf78`). One memory+ layer is added to the first MLA layer's MoE output (layer 3):
- 262,144 slots (512² product keys), with qk-normed queries and top-k over each half-key, then over the k² candidate sums.
- The value table (134M parameters) is shared by the heads, row-sharded like the bigram table, with Adam at 4× LR.
- The output is SiLU-gated, with a zero-init output projection.

It logs slot coverage, usage entropy, top-1 score and weight, and the output-projection norm as `train/attn_res/knob_mem_*`. The estimated cost is +5–8 ms per step at 2 heads × top-16 and +15–25 ms at 4×32, so the loss gain has to beat roughly 0.005 and 0.015 respectively at fixed time.

**First results** (paired vs the same-commit candidate 6 rerun: 3.0060 / 3.0053 at 148.6 / 149.9 ms, 471 / 475 s; batch 80's were 3.0029 / 3.0046, a ~0.002 rerun spread)

| change | steps | median step | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | at fixed time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **routed experts 512 wide** | 3170 | 154 ms (+3.4%) | **2.9934** | **2.9939** | **−0.0120** | ≈ −0.006 (486–489 s, over budget) |
| shared expert 768 wide | 3170 | 155 ms (+4%) | 2.9998 | 2.9995 | −0.0060 | ≈ 0 |
| top-3, 3380 steps | 3380 | 142–145 ms | 3.0039 | 3.0008 | −0.0033 | ≈ −0.003 (481 / 490 s) |
| elementwise gated attention | 3170 | 148.6–153.5 ms | 3.0051 | 3.0084 | +0.0011 | ≈ 0 |

- **With top-4, the routed experts want to be wider.** Width 512 costs only 3.4% of step time and gains −0.012, the first results under 2.995. Top-4 × 512 is still less expert compute per token than top-8 × 384 (2048 vs 3072 units). So at fixed time, fewer and wider experts beat many narrow ones. This is the same direction as the ReLU² 1.5× width finding. Batch 82 maps this trade at fixed time.
- **A wider shared expert helps at equal steps but pays for itself in time.** Neutral at fixed time.
- **Top-3** continues the top-k plateau: within ~0.003 of top-4, slightly ahead. Seed 1 ran 2% over budget.
- **Elementwise gated attention is neutral.** The headwise gate already does the job on our two q/k-normed MLA layers. Closed.

**Product-key memory layer: used heavily, adds little, costs a lot.** Paired vs the candidate 6 rerun, at equal steps:

| config | Δ | median step | slots touched / step | usage entropy | top-1 weight | ‖W_out‖ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 heads × top-16 | −0.0019 / −0.0011 | 167–170 ms (+13%) | 65% | 0.66–0.68 | 0.21 | 84–87 |
| 4 heads × top-32 | −0.0049 / −0.0014 | 211 ms (+42%) | 99.7% | 0.88 | 0.12 | 81–83 |

- The model does use the memory: the zero-init output projection grows to norm ~85, and at 4×32 nearly every slot is read every step.
- But retrieval is diffuse: the top-1 weight is 0.12–0.21 over 32–128 rows. So the memory behaves like a wide extra FFN, not a sparse key-value lookup. Quadrupling the reads only doubles the gain (−0.0015 → −0.003).
- Our hashed bigram table already fills the token-keyed memory role, and the MoE supplies the FFN capacity.
- At fixed time both configs lose badly (≈ +0.02 and +0.07). The step cost is dominated by the bag gather/scatter over a 134M-row table, well above the 5–8 ms estimate.
- **Closed.**

comments.body: The current hero on main uses a near dropless ragged all to all. If we could get that working here on H100 it would probably help a lot.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 On it. What I found so far about the hero's ragged transport:
- It depends on XLA's device-initiated ragged-all-to-all kernel (`--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel`), which needs Marin's patched `jax-cuda13-pjrt`. That wheel is aarch64 / GB200-only.
- Its expert MLP is SM100-specialized.
- `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py` is already in this branch, but it assumes gated SwiGLU experts. Our d512 experts are ungated ReLU².

An agent is now:
1. checking whether stock x86 XLA on H100 runs `ragged_all_to_all` (the NCCL decomposition, or the device kernel), and whether an x86 build of the patched PJRT is feasible;
2. adding a `moe_implementation` switch to fast_track, with ungated ReLU² support in the ragged path;
3. testing ragged vs pooled-wave on a CPU mesh, and writing a one-layer H100 microbenchmark (pooled-wave vs ragged at the d512 shapes).

I'll run the benchmark first. A full d512 run is only worth it if the ragged transport is faster on H100.

- **ReLU² 1.5× experts** (candidate 2; back to SwiGLU 256 routed and shared). At d768 this already measured k 1.028×.

comments.body:
Hmm. the current d512 target can be gamed by MFU chasing on the 8xH100 box- as seen in nanogpt if you want the best 8xH100 time, you way oversize the model, because bigger matmuls get better MFU. The relative gain here shrinks at scale once the matmuls get big enough to saturate the GPU. Our original baseline was 8 active of 384. To counteract the gaming, lets make sure that our d1024 always fits on 8xH100, and that expert sizes and shared sizes scale with hidden_dim. Long term we will counteract the gaming fully by measuring MFU on hero scale.

One change that typically helps is raising sparsity (right now we are 384/8=48) ratio of 64 usually does better.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 86: sparsity 64, and widths as multiples of hidden_dim that must fit at d1024** (replying to [your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451) on MFU gaming)

Agreed: batch 85's routed-width gains partly buy more FLOPs per token, and at d512 bigger matmuls also run at better MFU, which won't carry to hero scale. From here on:
- **Expert widths are stated as multiples of hidden_dim.** Candidate 6 is routed 0.75d × 8 + shared 0.75d. Batch 85's best compute-bounded shape, routed 1024 / shared 192 at d512, is **routed 2d / shared 0.375d**.
- **A shape is only adoptable if the same ratios fit at d1024 on 8×H100.** Below are 40-step d1024 memory probes for each shape. The d768 width checks already queued (routed 1024 vs 1536 = 2d, shared 288 = 0.375d) test the scaled version.
- **Sparsity 64:** 512 experts, top-8, at candidate 6 widths and at the 2d / 0.375d shape. EP is 8-way, so that's 64 local experts per GPU.

Also from batches 84 and 85 (d768, 1 seed), on your earlier scale-with-scale point:
- EMA scaled to steps: **−0.0042**.
- Bigram 1M: −0.0042; bigram 2M: **−0.0091**.
- EMA + bigram 1M: −0.0070.
- The two leave-one-out pieces that stopped helping at d768 were AdEMAMix (its horizon now scaled in a d768 run) and the bigram gate (possibly table-size-bound). A d512 bigram-1M check is running too.

**Bigram 1M rows at d512** (candidate 6 top-8, equal steps): **3.0019 / 3.0068, i.e. −0.0053 / −0.0041 (mean −0.0047)**, at 180.4 / 182.8 ms vs 176.7 / 178.2 ms (+2.5%).
- At d512 fixed time that's roughly break-even. But the same doubling paid −0.0042 at d768, and 2M rows paid −0.0091 there.
- The table's cost is a sparse gather/scatter plus Adam on its rows, and it shrinks relative to the dense compute as width grows.
- So the recipe should size the bigram table by training tokens rather than holding 524k fixed. 2M at d512 is in batch 87.

**Results**

**Sparsity 64 (512 experts, top-8) at candidate 6 widths: 2.9959 / 3.0017, i.e. −0.0113 / −0.0092 (mean −0.010)**, at 179.3 / 180.2 ms (+1.5%) and 35.8 GiB peak (the same as 384 experts). The biggest single equal-step win in a while, and it doesn't densify. Next (batch 88): 1 shared expert instead of 2, on top of 512 experts.

**d1024 memory probes** (40 steps; XLA memory limit 59.4 GiB per GPU):

| d1024 shape | peak GiB | fits? |
|---|---|---|
| routed 0.75d / shared 2×0.75d (candidate 6) | 55.7 | yes, barely |
| routed 1.5d / shared 2×0.375d | 64.2 | **no** |
| routed 2d / shared 2×0.375d | 74.2 | **no** |
| 512 experts, routed 2d / shared 2×0.375d | OOM | **no** |

- **Under the d1024-must-fit rule, batch 85's routed-width gains (up to −0.038 at routed 1280) aren't adoptable as configured.** At d1024 only 0.75d fits, with ~4 GiB of headroom.
- So the adoptable MoE direction right now is **more experts at 0.75d (sparsity 64)** plus shrinking shared.
- A d1024 probe of 512 experts at 0.75d is queued. It adds 33% expert parameters, so fitting may need a memory lever: the expert-parameter share of HBM, or optimizer-state offload as on the hero.

**512 experts × routed 2d / shared 2×0.375d: 2.9659 / 2.9720**, i.e. −0.0071 / −0.0071 vs the same widths at 384 experts (2.9730 / 2.9791), and **−0.040 vs candidate 6**. 203.7 ms, 48.5 GiB at d512. So the sparsity gain stacks with routed width. This shape doesn't fit at d1024 as-is.

On [the backward-policy suggestion](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451): d1024 already runs with `attn_res_layer_backward=recompute` (only d512 uses SAVE), so the probes above were at the low-memory backward already. The next memory lever is `attn_res_remat_attention=true`, which d1280 already needs. d1024 probes with it are queued for routed 1.5d, routed 2d, and 512 experts at 0.75d. If none fits, the next levers are the KDA chunk-state save policy and an optimizer-state offload.

- **Gated value embeddings** (b01/b02: −0.0025, 1 seed, on the fp32-fix base). Batch 77's value residual found L5 wants token-identity values (λ2 ≈ 3.0 vs λ1 ≈ 0.3). A version at the bigram table's ×10 LR needs a small routing change and comes next.
- **Bigram 2M rows, and 2M at LR ×20** (1M gave −0.022 in b50 but was rejected for −4.5% ex/s before `embed2_fsdp` made the table cheap; at d768, 2M gave −0.0091 without saturating). 1M at d512 is already running in batch 86.

- **NoPE MLA, i.e. no Inkling rel-pos** (b11: +0.0033, on the qk 2.5 base, before the partial key offset and q/k norms).
- **EP capacity 1.3** (only 1.0 was tried, at +0.12; a curve that steep suggests 1.15 may still drop too many tokens).

A parallel literature scout is collecting new papers for the next batch. Ideas it judged well explored and negative (DyT, PLE, product-key memory, MoE++, Grokfast and others) aren't retried.

| revisit | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | median step |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **gated value embeddings (1× LR)** | **2.9986** | **2.9986** | **−0.0105** | 178 ms (+0.5%) |
| bigram 2M rows | 3.0010 | 3.0010 | **−0.0081** | 189 ms (+7%) |
| bigram 2M rows, LR ×20 | 3.0027 | 3.0062 | −0.0046 | 188 ms |
| AttnRes V gate | 3.0027 | 3.0059 | −0.0048 | 187 ms (+6%) |
| AttnRes 4 heads + V gate | 3.0038 | 3.0083 | −0.0030 | 183 ms |
| EP capacity 1.3 | 3.0040 | 3.0083 | −0.0029 | 185 ms (+4.5%) |

| OKLS on all attention | 3.0077 | (rerun) | +0.0005 (seed 0) | 198 ms |
| NoPE MLA (no Inkling) | 3.0087 | 3.0128 | +0.0017 | 173 ms (−2%) |
| SNOO K=50, η 0.3 | 3.0396 | 3.0460 | **+0.034** | 180 ms |
| SNOO K=20, η 0.3 | (running) | 3.0486 | +0.038 | 180 ms |

- **Gated value embeddings were the clearest missed chance.** Batch 1 had them at −0.0025 on one seed; on the current recipe they give −0.0105 on both seeds, nearly free. That's consistent with batch 77's value-residual finding (the last MLA layer takes ~90% of its values from layer 0): the MLA layers want token-identity values. The ×10-LR version is queued.
- **Bigram 2M at d512 helps, but at the table's current LR** (×10). ×20 is worse. Seed 0 is still pending.
- **AttnRes V gate:** −0.005 on both seeds, but +6% step time. The multi-head combination (b24's −0.0115) doesn't replicate: −0.003.
- **Closed:** SNOO (+0.034 / +0.038 on the current recipe; not diagnosed further, but an outer step that pulls weights off the MuonH hyperball is a plausible cause), OKLS on attention (neutral), and NoPE MLA (+0.0017 at equal steps, −2% time, so ≈ neutral at fixed time, but slightly behind Inkling at equal steps).
- Two runs failed on a node with a corrupted package cache (`scipy._lib._array_api` ImportError, around 04:20 UTC) and were requeued.

**EP capacity 1.3: −0.0032 / −0.0026.** It drops 0.4% / 1.1% of expert assignments, against **1.3% for the base at 1.15**. So candidate 6 still loses ~1.3% of its routed compute to capacity drops, worth ≈ 0.003. That's more reason to get the near-dropless ragged transport running on H100 (0.018% drops on the hero), rather than paying +4.5% step time for bigger fixed buffers.

**Dense router gradient: +0.065 / +0.034** (3.0721 / 3.0453, 183 ms). Much worse than on batch 45's base (−0.003). Its stateless default-expert term (the stand-in for the paper's EMA of expert outputs) apparently doesn't suit the current ungated-ReLU² experts; not diagnosed further. Closed unless the EMA version is built.

**Adam β2 0.99, seed 1: 3.0078 (−0.0031)**, with seed 0 rerunning. **OKLS on all attention, seed 1: 3.0112 (+0.0003)**, neutral on both seeds, so it's closed.

**Adam β2 0.999: +0.0049 / +0.0048** (3.0121 / 3.0158), against β2 0.99 at −0.0031 (seed 1; seed 0 rerunning). A longer second-moment horizon hurts and a shorter one may help, the same direction AdEMAMix's short β3 favoured.

**MoE latent 384 (0.75d): ≈ −0.02 on seed 1 (2.9903, final pending), but 203 ms (+14%). Not adopted.** Per the owner, the latent stays at 0.5 × hidden_dim for MFU reasons at hero scale. Recorded as a rule alongside "d1024 must fit" and "widths scale with hidden_dim".

**Gated value embeddings at table LR ×10: −0.0059 / +0.0014 (mean −0.0023)** vs −0.0105 at 1× LR. The value tables want the plain Adam LR.

**Bigram 2M rows, seed 0: 3.0010 (−0.0062)**, so −0.0062 / −0.0099 (mean −0.0081) for +7% step time. **Cosine schedule: −0.0028 / −0.0020 (mean −0.0024).** It still helps on top of the MuonH decay power (the `lr_schedule` flag changes the Adam groups' schedule, and MuonH keeps its power-0.7 decay). Small, consistent, and free, so it goes to the next consolidation.

**Adam β2 0.99, seed 0: 3.0040 (−0.0032)**, so −0.0032 / −0.0031 (mean **−0.0031**), free, against +0.0049 for 0.999. The heuristic's 0.996 is too long a horizon for this run. Bracketing 0.98 / 0.95 in batch 89. It goes to the next consolidation.

🤖 **Batch 88 (being implemented): new papers.** A literature scout checked papers against what's already in `model.py` / `optimizer.py`, and these are now being implemented in parallel, each as a default-off flag with learned-knob logging:

| idea | paper | change |
|---|---|---|
| KDA output correction | Comba, arXiv 2506.02475 | read with q − d·k (learnable d per head); closes the delta rule's feedback loop; ~free |
| MLA value noise filter | arXiv 2609.22005 | per-head key-side gate σ(wᵀv + b)·v on MLA values; gain reported to grow 10M→350M |
| zero-centered norm gains + decay | Qwen3.8-Next, arXiv 2608.30320 §2.1.1 | gains as 1+γ, weight decay on γ |
| expert–router coupling loss | ERC, arXiv 2512.23447 | ties router rows to expert function; cost independent of tokens |
| next implicit token prediction | NITP, arXiv 2605.24956 | cosine aux loss predicting the next token's shallow representation (dense target, unlike the failed discrete MTP) |
| data-dependent rotation in KDA | Mamba-3 2603.15569, Selective RoPE 2511.17388 | complex-eigenvalue transitions via input-dependent q/k rotation, with decay tied per rotated pair |
| GDN-2 erase gate | arXiv 2605.22791 | channel-wise erase key b⊙k in the delta rule (kernel change); the paper's ablation says the erase half is what matters; checking whether PKDA (2604.21100) comes for free |
| Newton-Muon on experts | arXiv 2604.01472 | Muon update right-preconditioned by the expert-input covariance (one 256×256 per layer, shared by all experts) |

So most channels erase harder than plain KDA's β allows (b ∈ (0, 2) acts as a per-channel multiplier on β). The gain is modest but consistent, and nearly free. A candidate for the next consolidation once the erase-only seed 1 lands.

- **Value noise filter:** neutral. Its gate statistics didn't reach W&B (the MLA stats path apparently drops them on this model), so there's no diagnosis of whether the gate moved off its ≈0.98 init. Closed unless the stats are fixed.
- **Zero-centered gains:** neutral, as expected; the paper's claim is stability under LR stress, not loss at a stable LR. Closed for d512.

**Erase gate alone, seed 1: 3.0096 (−0.0013)**, so −0.0021 / −0.0013 (mean −0.0017). Erase + write (−0.0024) is the version to carry.
